title: Three strangers at the tent (Genesis 18:1–8)
hookLine: Abraham, still healing, runs in the heat to welcome three travelers

cards: By now Abram has a new name: Abraham. He's ninety-nine, and he has just been circumcised, as the sign of God's covenant. He's healing.
In the old JPS translation, the scene opens like this: "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day."
The heat of the day: the hour when sensible people stay put. An old man sits in the shade of his doorway, sore. He looks up and sees three men standing near him.
It's the doorbell ringing at the worst possible moment. And Abraham doesn't just get up. He runs.

teach.b: Hachnasat orchim. Literally, bringing in the guests: the Hebrew name for hospitality, and the rabbis point to this scene as its model. Watch the verbs.
He runs to meet them. He bows. He hurries into the tent to Sarah: quick, three measures of fine flour, make cakes.
He runs to the herd for a tender calf. The servant hurries to prepare it. For an old man, still healing, in the heat, that's a lot of running.
And listen to what he promises: just a little water to wash your feet, rest under the tree, and "a morsel of bread." Then he serves fresh cakes, a whole calf, curds and milk.
The sage Shammai taught, say little and do much, and the Talmud points to Abraham here as the example. The rabbis also asked: what was God doing there?
The chapter opens with God appearing, and then Abraham turns away to the strangers. The Talmud reads it as God visiting the sick, coming to Abraham as he healed.
And it draws a startling lesson: when the travelers came, Abraham asked God to wait.
So, the Talmud says, welcoming guests is greater even than receiving the Divine Presence.

teach.h: A TENT OPEN ON FOUR SIDES.
teach.b: There's also a tradition that Abraham's tent was open on all four sides, so a traveler from any direction would find a door. Nobody had to knock. The guests, the story later shows, were angels.
But Abraham didn't know that when he ran. To him, they were just three tired strangers in the heat.

how: Jewish tradition counts welcoming guests as a mitzvah, a commandment: inviting travelers, students and people alone to a Shabbat or holiday meal is a common way it's done.

a blessing said before a shared meal

games.q: you're Abraham, ninety-nine and healing, sitting in the shade in the heat of the day. three strangers appear. what do you do?
o: stay seated and wave them in.
run to meet them and bring them in.
wait to see if they're important.
games.why: he runs, bows, promises a morsel of bread, then serves cakes, a calf, curds and milk. promise little, do much.

practice: Think of the doorways in your life, your front door, your desk, your table, the empty seat next to you, and someone who might come through one today: a coworker, a delivery driver, a neighbor, a new kid at school, a relative.
Picture offering them something small, a glass of water, a chair, a coffee, five minutes, quickly, before they have to ask. If you pray, you can ask for an open door.

wordCard.voice: Hachnasat orchim. Bringing in guests. Abraham's hospitality, running in the heat, and a mitzvah, a commandment, in Jewish life.

orig.note: Hebrew: bringing in guests. the Jewish name for hospitality.

carryVoice: Your line: run to the guest. He promised bread and brought a feast. Until tomorrow.
